processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Ingots with nominal composition Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu (at.%) produced by melting high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials in a vacuum induction furnace under argon; alloy designated 17Al.
Hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm.
Plates cut into 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ samples for Vickers hardness measurements and microstructure characterizations.
Solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under argon followed by oil quenching (parent process proc_st-1100c-10min-oq).
This sample is the 17Al alloy aged at 575 °C for 1 h, followed by water quenching (one of the 525–650 °C / 1,3,6,10 h aging matrix).

characterization_methods.key_findings: 17Al alloy aged at 575 °C for 1 h has a Vickers hardness of 438.1 ± 39.3 HV.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: load 9.8 N for 15 s; 5 repeated measurements averaged per sample
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure Vickers hardness of the aged samples

characterization_methods.key_findings: Both α-Mn and β-Mn diffraction peaks were found in the pattern (red trace, 17Al 575 °C × 1 h), alongside α/D0₃ reflections, indicating α-Mn and β-Mn co-precipitated before the α matrix fully transformed to β-Mn.
characterization_methods.purpose: Identify constituent phases of the 17Al alloy aged at 575 °C for 1 h (one of three samples selected for XRD)

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: ZEISS Sigma 300 SEM operated at 5 kV
characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 575 °C/1 h panel, elongated/needle-like contrast within the α matrix indicates a largely untransformed structure; only a small amount of β-Mn is resolved.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: electrolytically polished samples (10 % perchloric acid + 90 % ethanol); 50 µm main-field scale bars
characterization_methods.purpose: Observe precipitation of α-Mn and β-Mn in the 17Al alloy after different aging treatments

interfaces.interface_notes: For this sample (17Al, 575 °C/1 h) only α/β-Mn interfaces from the onset of β-Mn precipitation are documented. The fine FCC Cu-rich and new BCC phases reported to decorate the β-Mn interfaces (Figs. 4–6, 11, 12) were characterized in the fully transformed, hardest states (e.g. 17Al 575 °C/6 h), not in the 1 h condition. The general aging sequence given by the paper is α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase.
interfaces.phase_evolution: α → α + α-Mn + β-Mn (at the 575 °C/1 h stage the α matrix is only partially transformed, with β-Mn nucleating at α grain boundaries and within α grains)

phases_present.phase_name: α (BCC, with D0₃-type ordering contributions in XRD)

phases_present.morphology: short rod-shaped; precipitated along α grain boundaries and within α grains
small particles in the α matrix

precipitates.distribution: along α grain boundaries and within α grains (small amount after 1 h)
in the α matrix as fine particles

microstructure_list.region: bulk (α grain boundaries and α grain interiors)

structures.overall_structure: Aged 575 °C/1 h state of the 17Al (Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu) alloy: the α (BCC) matrix is largely untransformed with only a small amount of β-Mn precipitated along α grain boundaries and within the α grains; SE images of this condition show elongated/needle-like contrast within the α matrix (untransformed structure). XRD of this exact sample shows α/D0₃ together with both α-Mn and β-Mn reflections.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Vickers microhardness measured on an HVS-1000 digital microhardness tester with a load of 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample tested 5 times and the value given as the average of 5 measurements.

unmapped_findings: 17Al alloy composition (EDS, Table 1): Fe 43.2, Mn 34.8, Al 17.0, Cu 5.0 (at.%); measured density = 6.76 g/cm³ (Archimedes method). This is the alloy used for this sample.
The solution-treated 17Al baseline Vickers hardness (parent proc_st-1100c-10min-oq state) is 259.8 ± 1.5 HV (Table 3); all aged conditions far exceed this baseline.

The 575 °C × 1 h hardness of 17Al (438.1 ± 39.3 HV) is the minimum entry in Table 3 and is lower than its 1 h values at 525 °C (566.9 ± 9.7 HV) and 550 °C (511.6 ± 15.6 HV); the paper notes hardness increases with aging time/temperature and that β-Mn precipitation kinetics slow down with increasing Al content.

Continued aging of the same 17Al alloy at 575 °C accelerates hardening: 811.7 ± 39.3 HV at 3 h and a peak of 924.9 ± 25.8 HV at 6 h, falling to 831.3 ± 27.4 HV at 10 h (Table 3); these are separate aging states, not the 1 h sample.

General aging microstructure evolution reported for Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase; the new BCC and FCC Cu-rich phases appear between β-Mn interfaces only after the α matrix has almost fully transformed to β-Mn.

For the 17Al alloy, EBSD of the fully transformed states (e.g. 575 °C/6 h, 650 °C/10 h) shows an almost pure β-Mn phase map; TEM of the 17Al alloy aged 575 °C for 6 h (Fig. 12) shows fine FCC Cu-rich particles with FCC twins at β-Mn interfaces. These characterizations correspond to the 6–10 h / higher-temperature states, not to the 1 h sample.

Nanoindentation of the hardest samples (Fig. 13) gives average nanohardness 11.7 ± 0.4 GPa (15Al), 11.1 ± 0.6 GPa (17Al) and 10.4 ± 1.3 GPa (19Al); β-Mn intrinsic hardness in the hardest samples is 12.1 ± 0.3 GPa (15Al), 12.2 ± 0.1 GPa (17Al) and 12.5 ± 0.4 GPa (19Al). β-Mn in the hardest 17Al sample contains Mn 36.2, Al 16.3, Cu 2.6 at.% by SEM-EDS (Fig. 14). These pertain to the 17Al peak-hardness (575 °C/6 h) state, not the 1 h sample.
